[[Association football|Football]] is the most popular [[sport in Argentina]] and part of the [[culture of Argentina|culture in the country]].<ref>According to the Wikipedia article [[Sport in Argentina]]</ref> It is the one with the most players (2,658,811 total, 331,811 of which are registered and 2,327,000 unregistered; with 3,377 clubs and 37,161 officials, all according to [[FIFA]])<ref name=fifa>[https://web.archive.org/web/20150102164538/http://www.fifa.com/associations/association=arg/countryInfo.html Country info] on FIFA website</ref> and is the most popular recreational sport, played from childhood into old age.<ref>Secretaría de Deportes de la Nación e INDEC; Censo sobre Hábitos en actividades físicas y deportivas de la población argentina, Buenos Aires, 2000.</ref> The percentage of Argentines that declare allegiance to an Argentine football club is about 90%.<ref>[http://www.consultoraequis.com/equisenlosmedios_ole_010406.htm Consulto Aequis] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919123223/http://www.consultoraequis.com/equisenlosmedios_ole_010406.htm |date=19 September 2008 }}</ref>

Football was introduced to Argentina in the latter half of the 19th century by the [[English settlement in Argentina|British immigrants]] in [[Buenos Aires]]. The first Argentine league was contested in [[1891 Argentine Primera División|1891]], making it the fifth-oldest recognised league of a [[FIFA]] member (after [[England]], [[Scotland]], [[Northern Ireland]] and the [[Netherlands]]).<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg1891.html Argentina 1891] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090228072450/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesa/arg1891.html |date=28 February 2009 }} at [[RSSSF]]</ref> The [[Argentine Football Association]] (AFA) was formed in 1893 and is the eighth-oldest in the world.

The [[Argentina national football team|Argentina national team]] is one of the eight to have won the [[FIFA World Cup]], having done so in [[1978 FIFA World Cup|1978]], [[1986 FIFA World Cup|1986]], and [[2022 FIFA World Cup|2022]], while being runner-up in [[1930 FIFA World Cup|1930]], [[1990 FIFA World Cup|1990]], [[2014 FIFA World Cup|2014]] and [[2026 FIFA World Cup|2026]]. Argentina has also won the top continental tournament, the [[Copa América]], 16 times, and the [[FIFA Confederations Cup]] in [[1992 King Fahd Cup|1992]]. It also holds the record for having more official titles than any other nation with 23. The nation's [[Argentina Olympic football team|Olympic representative]] has won two gold medals (in [[Football at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2004]] and [[Football at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2008]]), while the [[Argentina national under-20 football team|under-20 team]] has won a record six [[FIFA U-20 World Cup|U-20 World Cups]]. At club level, Argentine teams have won the most [[Intercontinental Cup (1960–2004)|Intercontinental Cups]] (9) and the most [[Copa Libertadores]] (25).

[[Women's association football|Women's football]] has a national league since 1991, the [[Campeonato de Fútbol Femenino]]. In turn, the [[Argentina women's national football team|female national representative]] qualified for the [[FIFA Women's World Cup|World Cup]] for the first time in [[2007 FIFA Women's World Cup|2007]] and won their first [[Campeonato Sudamericano Femenino]] (top continental competition) in [[2006 Sudamericano Femenino|2006]].

In [[futsal]], Argentina were [[FIFUSA/AMF Futsal World Cup]] champions in [[AMF Futsal World Cup|1994]] and [[AMF Futsal World Cup|2019]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.amfutsal.com.py/noticias/mundial-2019/argentina-es-campeon-del-mundo|title=ARGENTINA ES CAMPEÓN DEL MUNDO...! - Mundial 2019 - AMF|access-date=1 September 2019|archive-date=1 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190901140257/http://www.amfutsal.com.py/noticias/mundial-2019/argentina-es-campeon-del-mundo|url-status=dead}}</ref> They also compete in the FIFA code of futsal, where they finished champions in [[2016 FIFA Futsal World Cup|2016]], runner-up in [[2021 FIFA Futsal World Cup|2021]] and fourth place in [[2004 FIFA Futsal World Championship|2004]].<ref name="es.fifa.com">[https://web.archive.org/web/20190901140254/https://es.fifa.com/futsalworldcup/teams/team%3D1883214/profile-detail.html FIFA.com]</ref> The team also won the FIFA Futsal Copa América in [[2003 Copa América de Futsal|2003]], [[2015 Copa América de Futsal|2015]] and [[2022 Copa América de Futsal|2022]].<ref name="es.fifa.com"/> Moreover, Argentina was world champion in [[Paralympic association football|futsal for the visually impaired]] in [[World Blind Football Championships|2002]], [[World Blind Football Championships|2006]] and [[World Blind Football Championships|2023]], and also won the gold medal at the IBSA World Blind Games [[World Blind Football Championships|2015]], a silver medal ([[Argentina at the 2004 Summer Paralympics|2004]]) and two Bronze ([[Argentina at the 2008 Summer Paralympics|2008]] and [[Argentina at the 2016 Summer Paralympics|2016]]) in the Paralympic Games, three runner-up world championships ([[World Blind Football Championships|1998]], [[World Blind Football Championships|2000]] and [[World Blind Football Championships|2014]]), three championships of the Copa América (1999, 2005, 2017), three silver medals in the Parapan American Games ([[Football 7-a-side at the 2007 Parapan American Games|2007]], [[Football 5-a-side at the 2011 Parapan American Games|2011]], [[Football 7-a-side at the 2015 Parapan American Games|2015]]) and two runner-up finishes in the Copa América (2009 and 2013).

Argentina also compete in the [[beach football]] [[FIFA Beach Soccer World Cup|World Cup]], where their best finish was third in 2001.<ref>[http://www.afa.org.ar/index.php?m=news&n=1343&idm=20 AFA - Fútbol Playa] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110531183333/http://www.afa.org.ar/index.php?m=news&n=1343&idm=20 |date=31 May 2011 }} {{in lang|es}}</ref>

==History==

=== The beginning ===
{{main|History of football in Argentina (1867–1899)}}
[[File:Football match the standard 1867.jpg|thumb|90px|The first football match played in Argentina, as covered by ''[[Buenos Aires Standard|The Standard]]'', June 1867]]
By 1867, there was a large British community in Buenos Aires. Most of them had established themselves in Argentina coming from the United Kingdom as managers and workers of the British-owned railway companies that operated in Argentina. British citizens founded social and sports clubs where they could practise their sports, such as [[bowls]], [[cricket]], [[association football|football]], [[golf]], [[horse riding]], [[rugby union]] and [[tennis]] amongst others.

[[file:Campo_ba_cricket_club.jpg|thumb|left|230px|The [[Buenos Aires Cricket Club Ground]] in [[Palermo, Buenos Aires]] held the first football match on 20 June 1867]]
Two English immigrants, Thomas and James Hogg, organized a meeting on 9 May 1867 in Buenos Aires where the [[Buenos Aires Football Club]] was founded. The club was given permission by the [[Buenos Aires Cricket Club]] to make use of the cricket field in [[Parque Tres de Febrero]], [[Palermo, Buenos Aires]], on the site now occupied by the [[Galileo Galilei planetarium]]. The first recorded football match in Argentina took place on this pitch on 20 June 1867,<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg-early-info.html ''Early History of Football in Argentina''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923230520/https://rsssf.org/tablesa/arg-early-info.html |date=2022-09-23 }} - [[Rec.sport.soccer Statistics Foundation|RSSSF]] by Osvaldo J. Georgazzi, 1999</ref> being covered by [[English language]] daily newspaper ''[[Buenos Aires Standard|The Standard]]''. This newspaper, published in Argentina, was the first one to cover football matches in the country.<ref name="iwa">{{cite book |last=Iwanczuk |first=Jorge |title=Historia del Fútbol Amateur en la Argentina |title-link=Historia del Fútbol Amateur en la Argentina |date=1992 |publisher=[[Centro para la Investigación de la Historia del Fútbol]] |isbn=978-950-43-4384-4 |edition=1st |language=es |trans-title=History of amateur football in Argentina}}</ref> That first match, originally scheduled for May 25 in [[La Boca]], had to be postponed due to bad weather.<ref name=gallego>[https://www.telam.com.ar/notas/201706/192897-150-anos-primer-partido-futbol-argentina.html 150 años del primer partido de fútbol en Argentina] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201025201742/https://www.telam.com.ar/notas/201706/192897-150-anos-primer-partido-futbol-argentina.html |date=2020-10-25 }} by Jorge Gallego on Telam, 20 June 2017</ref>

=== Early 20th. century ===
{{main|History of football in Argentina (1900–1919)}}
[[file:Alumni_1906champion.jpg|thumb|left|230px|Team of [[Alumni Athletic Club|Alumni]] that defeated South Africa in 1906. The Southafricans were one of several British teams that toured Argentina in the 20th. century]]
The most successful and admired team of this early period was [[Alumni Athletic Club|Alumni]], founded by graduates and students of [[Alexander Watson Hutton|Watson Hutton's]] English High School. Like all of the early clubs, it was composed mainly of British players.

Towards the end of the 19th century, the game became increasingly popular amongst other European immigrants, especially Italians.

[[United Kingdom|British]] [[football club (association football)|football clubs]] [[British football clubs tours to South America|tours of South America]] contributed to the spread and development of football in Argentina during the first years of the 20th century. The first club to tour the country was [[Southampton F.C.]] in 1904, who were captained by [[George Molyneux|George Molyneaux]]. They beat the Buenos Aires High School Alumni team 3-0 with Molyneaux remarking on 'how far the Argentines were ahead of their European counterparts in France and Denmark.'<ref>{{Cite book|last=Archetti|first=Eduardo|title=Masculinities: Football, Polo, and the Tango in Argentina|publisher=Berg|year=1999|isbn=1-85973-266-6|location=Oxford|pages=50–51}}</ref> Several other teams came afterwards (mainly from England although some Scottish clubs also visited South America), until 1929 with [[Chelsea F.C.]] being the last team to tour.<ref name=chelseatour>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesc/chelsea-satrip29.html South American Trip of Chelsea FC 1929] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210912071302/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesc/chelsea-satrip29.html |date=2021-09-12 }} by Pablo Ciullini on RSSSF</ref> 

In [[South American Championship 1916|1916]], [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]] competed in the first [[Copa América]] which was won by [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguay]]. [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]] would win the tournament for the first time in [[South American Championship 1921|1921]], and have gone on to win it a total of 16 times.

=== Consolidation ===
During the 1920s decade, [[Club Atlético Huracán|Huracan]] was a strong competitor, winning most of the annual championships, as [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing Club]] did during the 1910s. To mention a tradition, the Huracán footballers and fans used to meet at the historical [[:es:Café El Japonés|Japanese Cafe]].

In [[Football at the 1928 Summer Olympics|1928]], [[Argentina Olympic football team]] competed at the [[Football at the 1928 Summer Olympics|1928 Olympics]] in [[Amsterdam]], where they finished runners-up to [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguay]]. Two years later, they competed in the first [[FIFA World Cup]], again finishing runners up to hosts Uruguay.

Following two seasons of disrupted play due to mass cancellation and suspension of matches and the mid-season withdrawal of teams in the 1929,<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg29.html 1929 in Argentine football] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510090618/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesa/arg29.html |date=May 10, 2008 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref> and 1930,<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg30.html 1930 in Argentine football] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190407025644/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesa/arg30.html |date=2019-04-07 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref> 18 teams decided to form a breakaway professional league for the [[1931 Argentine Primera División|1931 season]].<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg31.html 1931 in Argentine football] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130610064448/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesa/arg31.html |date=2013-06-10 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref> The amateur league carried on in parallel until it folded in 1934 with many of the teams joining the new professional second division<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/arg2champ.html Argentine 2nd division champions] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516012626/http://www.rsssf.com/tablesa/arg2champ.html |date=2008-05-16 }} at [[rsssf]].</ref> The creation of the professional league helped curb the exodus of Argentine talent to high paying European football clubs. The [[1934 FIFA World Cup|1934 World Cup]] Italy national team championship side featured several ''[[Oriundo]]'' in the squad composed of Argentine-born players such as [[Raimundo Orsi]], [[Enrique Guaita]], and [[Luis Monti]] who also played for Argentina in the [[1930 FIFA World Cup|1930 World Cup]].

In [[Copa Libertadores 1964|1964]], [[Club Atlético Independiente|Independiente]] became the first Argentine club to win the [[Copa Libertadores]], Argentine clubs have won the competition a total of 25 times.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.conmebol.com/es/historia-copa-libertadores|title=Copa Libertadores. Historia &#124; CONMEBOL|date=24 January 2015|access-date=1 September 2019|archive-date=24 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190824112654/http://conmebol.com/es/historia-copa-libertadores|url-status=live}}</ref>

In [[1967 Intercontinental Cup|1967]], [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing]] became the first Argentine team to win the [[Intercontinental Cup (1960–2004)|Intercontinental Cup]]. Argentine clubs have won the tournament a record 9 times.<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablest/toyota.html Intercontinental Cup] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220812151601/https://www.rsssf.org/tablest/toyota.html |date=2022-08-12 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref>

In [[1971 Argentine Primera División|1971]], [[Rosario Central]] became the first club not based in Buenos Aires or [[Greater Buenos Aires]] to win the First Division League, after winning this year´s [[Nacional championship]].

In [[1978 FIFA World Cup|1978]], Argentina hosted the [[1978 FIFA World Cup|World Cup]], where the team defeated the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]] 3–1 [[after extra time]] in [[1978 FIFA World Cup Final|the final]] to win their first World Cup.

In [[1979 FIFA World Youth Championship|1979]], a young [[Diego Maradona]] was part of the [[Argentina national under-20 football team|Argentina under-20 team]] which won the [[FIFA U-20 World Cup|FIFA Under-20 World Cup]]. Argentina have gone on to win a record six U-20 World Cups.<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesw/wycall.html Under 20 World Cup] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240713160628/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesw/wycall.html |date=2024-07-13 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref>

In 1982, due to an uncertain political atmosphere and an extremely unstable government with multiple presidents over the span of a short time, most football clubs were lacking the money to keep top domestic players. 1982 saw a whole slew of players leave Argentina for Europe: players like Diego Maradona, [[Mario Kempes]] (who had already played in Spain and had briefly returned to Argentina), [[Daniel Passarella]] and many others leave for Spain, France, Italy or England.

In [[1986 FIFA World Cup|1986]], Argentina would win their second World Cup in the [[1986 FIFA World Cup|1986 World Cup]], where the team defeated to [[Germany national football team|Germany]] 3–2.

In [[1995 Copa CONMEBOL|1995]], [[Rosario Central]] became the first club not based in [[Buenos Aires]] or [[Greater Buenos Aires]] to win an international cup recognised by FIFA, the [[Copa Conmebol|Conmebol Cup]]. Argentine clubs have won the tournament a record three times.<ref>[[Copa CONMEBOL]]</ref>

In [[Football at the 2004 Summer Olympics|2004]], the [[Argentina Olympic football team]] won Gold at the [[2008 Summer Olympics|Athens Olympic games]]; they defended their title in [[Football at the 2008 Summer Olympics|2008]] to become the first team to defend the Olympic football title since Hungary in 1968.<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tableso/olympics.html Olympic football tournament] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711203909/https://www.rsssf.org/tableso/olympics.html |date=2022-07-11 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref>

In [[2022 FIFA World Cup|2022]], Argentina won the World Cup for the third time, beating [[France national football team|France]] 4–2 on penalties following a 3–3 draw after extra time.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.fifa.com/fifaplus/en/match-centre/match/17/255711/285077/400128145 |access-date=2022-12-18 |website=www.fifa.com |title=Archived copy |archive-date=2022-12-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221218153321/https://www.fifa.com/fifaplus/en/match-centre/match/17/255711/285077/400128145 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Clubs ==

=== League system ===
{{main|Argentine football league system}}

Around 520 registered football clubs play in the [[Argentine Football Association]] (AFA) league system, which is organized in a pyramid of seven leagues divided from the third level between ''clubs directly affiliated to AFA ([[:es:Anexo:Clubes directamente afiliados a la AFA|es]])'' and ''clubs indirectly affiliated to AFA ([[:es:Anexo:Clubes indirectamente afiliados a la AFA|es]])''. In the branch of clubs indirectly affiliated to AFA below the fourth level, there are 250 other [[List of regional football leagues in Argentina|Regional Leagues]] that are affiliated with AFA and compete for the right to enter the league system at the lowest tier.

The [[Argentine Primera División|Primera División]] is the highest level of club football in Argentina. It was founded in [[1891 Argentine Primera División|1891]] as an amateur competition, becoming professional in [[1931 Argentine Primera División|1931]] with a league by 18 teams which were dissatisfied with the amateur system they were participating on until [[1930 in Argentine football|1930]]. This group of 18 founding members of the present league included nearly all of the most prominent clubs of those times, unified by the idea that full and compulsory amateurism was no longer sustainable (many of those teams are still today among the most popular clubs in Argentina). For many years, the only winners were the so-called "[[The Big Five of Argentine football|big five]]"<ref name="Argentina - List of champions">[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/argchamp.html Argentina - List of champions] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230207205229/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/argchamp.html |date=2023-02-07 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref> ([[Boca Juniors]], [[Club Atlético Independiente|Independiente]], [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing Club]], [[Club Atlético River Plate|River Plate]] and [[San Lorenzo de Almagro]]). This dominance was finally broken in 1967 by [[Estudiantes de La Plata]]. Since then, ten other teams have won the championship, resulting in a total of 30 teams having been champions of Argentina as of 2026. River Plate has won the most championships with 38. The only teams outside the [[City of Buenos Aires|Buenos Aires]] and [[Greater Buenos Aires]] to have won the championship are [[Rosario Central]] and [[Newell's Old Boys]] from [[Rosario]], [[Estudiantes de La Plata|Estudiantes]] and [[Gimnasia y Esgrima de La Plata|Gimnasia y Esgrima]] from [[La Plata]] and [[Club Atlético Belgrano|Belgrano]] from [[Córdoba, Argentina|Córdoba]].

Below the second division, [[Primera B Nacional|Primera Nacional]], the league system is regionalized with three divisions for ''clubs directly affiliated to AFA ([[:es:Anexo:Clubes directamente afiliados a la AFA|es]])'' of [[City of Buenos Aires|Buenos Aires]], [[Greater Buenos Aires]] and twenty-two clubs from the cities of [[Rosario]], [[Santa Fe, Argentina|Santa Fe]], [[La Plata]], [[Zárate, Buenos Aires|Zarate]], [[Campana, Buenos Aires Province|Campana]], [[Luján, Buenos Aires|Luján]], [[Junín, Buenos Aires|Junín]], [[General Rodríguez]], [[Cañuelas]], [[Pilar, Buenos Aires Province|Pilar]] and [[Mercedes, Buenos Aires|Mercedes]]; and two divisions for ''clubs indirectly affiliated to AFA ([[:es:Anexo:Clubes indirectamente afiliados a la AFA|es]])'' that cover the rest of the country. Even below these seven leagues, Argentine football is regionalized into almost 250 [[List of regional football leagues in Argentina|Regional Leagues]], which consist of teams that participate in championships and tournaments organized by the Consejo Federal del Fútbol Argentino ([[:es:Consejo Federal del Fútbol Argentino|es]]) (CFFA), internal organ of the [[Argentine Football Association]] (AFA), to obtain the right to enter the [[Torneo Regional Federal Amateur]], established in 2018.

=== League championships ===
{{main|Argentine Primera División}}
The Primera División has been using different formats for its championships, from a double [[round-robin tournament]] (1891 to 1966) to a single round-robin that would become the standard in Latin America, the [[Apertura and Clausura]]. In the particular case of Argentina, the Apertura was contested in the second half of the calendar year, and the Clausura was played in the first half of the following year (in order to synchronize the seasons with those of the European football). Different formats used also included the organization of [[Metropolitano championship|Metropolitano]] and [[Nacional championship|Nacional]] championships, that lasted from 1967 to 1985.

As of [[2026 AFA Liga Profesional de Fútbol|2026 season]], the Argentine Primera División league is made up of 30 teams, with a championship organized in a single round-robin schedule, resulting in a total of 27 rounds per team. Six teams from Argentina are eligible to play the [[Copa Libertadores]], four from the league championship and the rest from the [[Copa Argentina]] and [[Copa de la Liga Profesional]]. The following six teams in the general table of the league championship are eligible to play the [[Copa Sudamericana]].

From 1891 to date, [[Club Atlético River Plate|River Plate]] is the most winning team with 38 domestic championships, followed by [[Boca Juniors]] with 35 titles. [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing]] holds the third position with 18 titles.

=== Domestic cups ===
{{main|List of Argentine football national cups}}

Since the creation of the first league in 1891, several cups have been played in Argentine apart from the main competition, the Primera División. The first cup held in the country was the [[Copa de Honor Municipalidad de Buenos Aires]]; first contested in 1905, it was played until 1936.<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/argcuphist.html Argentina - Domestic Cup History] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230202105413/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesa/argcuphist.html |date=2023-02-02 }} on [[RSSSF]]</ref>

As of the present, four domestic cups are held in Argentina: the [[Copa Argentina]], that includes teams of all divisions of Argentine football, and the [[Supercopa Argentina]] –contested by the reigning champions of Primera División and Copa Argentina, organised by the AFA. The third and fourth one are the [[Copa de la Liga Profesional]] and [[Trofeo de Campeones de la Liga Profesional|Trofeo de Campeones]], both organised by the Liga Profesional de Fútbol body. The annual football match was played for the first time in 2019, being played by the champions of [[Argentine Primera División|Primera División]] and [[Copa de la Superliga Argentina]] respectively.

The [[Copa Campeonato]], originally awarded to Primera División champion, is the oldest trophy of Argentine football,<ref name=oldest>[http://www.copaargentina.org/es/noticias/2948_El-trofeo-mas-anejo-del-futbol-argentino.html "El trofeo más añejo del fútbol argentino" at AFA website] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160915202341/http://www.copaargentina.org/es/noticias/2948_El-trofeo-mas-anejo-del-futbol-argentino.html |date=2016-09-15 }}, 26 Jun 2013</ref> having been established in 1896, three year after the AFA was created,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.afa.org.ar/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=7793&Itemid=128 |title=Orígenes de la Asociación on AFA website |access-date=2014-11-06 |archive-date=2014-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141130034740/http://www.afa.org.ar/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=7793&Itemid=128 |url-status=live }}</ref> and played without interruption until 1926.<ref name=memoria>{{Cite web |url=http://biblioteca.afa.org.ar/libros/libro_12/ |title=''Memoria y Balance 1935'' - Argentine Football Association Library |access-date=2014-11-06 |archive-date=2014-04-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407120250/http://biblioteca.afa.org.ar/libros/libro_12/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The Cup received several names, such as "Championship Cup", "Copa Campeonato", "Challenge Cup" and "Copa Alumni",<ref>[http://www.espndeportes.com/news/story?id=1834058&s=arg&type=story "Presentaron Superfinal Vélez-Newell's"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029160901/http://www.espndeportes.com/news/story?id=1834058&s=arg&type=story |date=2014-10-29 }} [[ESPN]]</ref> due to the association offered legendary team [[Alumni Athletic Club|Alumni]] to keep the Cup definitely for having won it three consecutive times (1900–02), but the club from [[Belgrano, Buenos Aires|Belgrano]] declined the honour to keep the trophy under dispute.<ref name=oldest/><ref>[http://www.diariouno.com.ar/deportes/Un-Copa-con-mucha-historia-20130627-0024.html "Una Copa con mucha historia", ''Diario Uno''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714131938/http://www.diariouno.com.ar/deportes/Un-Copa-con-mucha-historia-20130627-0024.html |date=2014-07-14 }}, 27 Jun 2013</ref>

All those competitions, although not considered league tournaments, are regarded as official titles.

=== Rivalries ===
{{main|Football rivalries in Argentina}}
There are many local rivalries in Argentine football. The most important is the [[Superclásico|''Superderby'']], which is contested between Argentina's two most popular<ref>[http://www.consultoraequis.com/Estudios_PDF/futbol_marzo06_.pdf Argentine football statistics PDF] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060624113018/http://www.consultoraequis.com/Estudios_PDF/futbol_marzo06_.pdf |date=2006-06-24 }}</ref> and successful<ref name="Argentina - List of champions"/> teams, [[Buenos Aires]] rivals [[Club Atlético River Plate|River Plate]] and [[Boca Juniors]]. The [[England|English]] newspaper ''[[The Observer]]'' put the ''superclásico'' (name in Spanish) at the top of their list of "The 50 Sporting Things You Must Do Before You Die".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/observer/osm/story/0,6903,1182710,00.html|title=50 sporting things you must do before you die|newspaper=[[The Observer]]|access-date=2008-12-08|archive-date=2013-06-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130616073708/http://observer.guardian.co.uk/osm/story/0,6903,1182710,00.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The second-most important rivalry in Argentine football is the ''[[Avellaneda derby]]'', which is contested between [[Club Atlético Independiente|Independiente]] and [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing]], the third- and fourth-most popular and third- and fourth-most successful teams of the country (respectively), both from the city of [[Avellaneda]] (located next to Buenos Aires, into it metropolitan area). Other important derbies include the derby between [[Club Atlético Huracán|Huracán]] and [[San Lorenzo de Almagro]] (has no particular denomination), the ''[[Rosario derby]]'' (between [[Newell's Old Boys]] and [[Rosario Central]]), the ''[[La Plata derby]]'' (between [[Estudiantes de La Plata]] and [[Gimnasia y Esgrima La Plata]]), the ''West derby'' (between [[Ferro Carril Oeste]] and [[Club Atlético Vélez Sársfield|Vélez Sarsfield]]), the derby between [[Club Atlético Atlanta|Atlanta]] and [[Chacarita Juniors]] (formerly denominated "Villa Crespo derby"), the ''[[Santa Fe derby]]'' (between [[Club Atlético Colón|Colón]] and [[Unión de Santa Fe|Unión]]), the ''North Zone derby'' (between [[Club Atlético Platense|Platense]] and [[Club Atlético Tigre|Tigre]]), the [[Clásico cordobés|''Cordoba derby'']] (between [[Belgrano de Córdoba|Belgrano]] and [[Talleres de Córdoba|Talleres]]), the derby between [[Instituto Atlético Central Córdoba|Instituto]] and [[Racing de Córdoba]] (has no particular denomination) and the ''Tucuman derby'' (between [[San Martín de Tucumán|San Martín]] and [[Atlético Tucumán]]).

=== Style of play ===
{{see also|Creole football}}
Circumstances allowed the wide development of a special style, called "pasture football", little regulated, often massive, without coaches, captains or parents. This includes a variety of football games, from more or less formal matches, to mass informal matches such as "el picado", or games such as "goal-goal-enter", the "loco", the "run", the " center-goal ", the" cañito-la liga ", the" football-tennis ", the" coca-cola ", the" head ", and so on. These conditions promoted a game based fundamentally on improvisation and individual skill in handling the ball, the so-called "art of dribbling" (dribbling), and the short pass, as well as a more physical and violent defensive game, with resource systematic to the old law of British premodern football, "hacking" or trip, known in the Río de la Plata as "ax".<ref>[https://www.unse.edu.ar/trabajoysociedad/Archetti.pdf ''El Deporte en Argentina (1914–1983)''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225140204/https://www.unse.edu.ar/trabajoysociedad/Archetti.pdf |date=2021-02-25 }} by Eduardo Archetti, University of Oslo</ref>

=== Clubs at international competitions ===
{{further|Qualifying method of Copa Libertadores in Argentina}}

The first international club competition was organized by both, [[Argentine Football Association|Argentine]] and [[Uruguayan Football Association|Uruguayan]] associations, with the establishment of [[Tie Cup]] or "Copa de Competencia Chevallier Boutell" in 1900. The tournament was held until 1919. Several competitions between teams from both countries followed, being the last the [[Copa Aldao]], which last edition was played in 1955.

The most successful Argentine club on the international stage is [[Boca Juniors]]. The club has won a total of 22 international titles.<ref>[https://www.clarin.com/deportes/futbol/titulos-internacionales-independiente_0_B1_H4qPBQ.html Independiente vs. Boca: quién tiene más títulos internacionales] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201206172225/https://www.clarin.com/deportes/futbol/titulos-internacionales-independiente_0_B1_H4qPBQ.html |date=2020-12-06 }} by Oscar Barnade, ''Clarín'', 8 Aug 2018</ref> Three of its wins are the [[Copa Intercontinental|Intercontinental Cup]] titles of [[1977 Intercontinental Cup|1977]], [[2000 Intercontinental Cup|2000]] and [[2003 Intercontinental Cup|2003]].<ref>[https://www.rsssf.org/tablest/toyota.html Intercontinental Cup] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220812151601/https://www.rsssf.org/tablest/toyota.html |date=2022-08-12 }} ar [[rsssf]]</ref>

[[Club Atlético Independiente|Independiente]] has won the most important continental title on the most occasions, its seven [[Copa Libertadores]] titles is a record, as is its feat of winning the title on four consecutive occasions (1972–75).<ref name="Copa Libertadores">[https://www.rsssf.org/sacups/copalib.html Copa Libertadores] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524152408/http://www.rsssf.com/sacups/copalib.html |date=2015-05-24 }} at [[rsssf]]</ref> Also, Independiente was the most successful club on international cups by more than twenty years. These achievements earned them the nickname of ''Rey de Copas (King of Cups)''.

A number of other Argentine clubs have won the Copa Libertadores, including [[Estudiantes de La Plata]] and [[Club Atlético River Plate|River Plate]] (four times each; [[Estudiantes de La Plata|Estudiantes]] in [[1968 Copa Libertadores|1968]], [[1969 Copa Libertadores|1969]], [[1970 Copa Libertadores|1970]], [[2009 Copa Libertadores|2009]] and [[Club Atlético River Plate|River Plate]] in [[1986 Copa Libertadores|1986]], [[1996 Copa Libertadores|1996]], [[2015 Copa Libertadores|2015]], [[2018 Copa Libertadores|2018]]), [[Racing Club de Avellaneda|Racing]] ([[1967 Copa Libertadores|1967]]), [[Argentinos Juniors]] ([[1985 Copa Libertadores|1985]]), [[Club Atlético Vélez Sarsfield|Vélez Sarsfield]] ([[1994 Copa Libertadores|1994]]) and [[San Lorenzo de Almagro|San Lorenzo]] ([[2014 Copa Libertadores|2014]]).

Some Argentine teams have won international titles without having won a [[Argentine Primera División|Primera División]] title, such as [[Talleres de Córdoba]] that won the [[Copa CONMEBOL]] in [[1999 Copa CONMEBOL|1999]], [[Arsenal de Sarandí]] winning the [[Copa Sudamericana]] in [[2007 Copa Sudamericana|2007]] (although the team then won a title, the [[2011–12 Argentine Primera División season|2012 Torneo Clausura]]) and [[Defensa y Justicia]] winning the [[Copa Sudamericana]] in [[2020 Copa Sudamericana|2020]].

== Culture ==
{{Tone|date=August 2026|section}}
Football plays an important part in the life of many Argentines. Even those supporters who usually do not attend the matches watch them on television and comment on them the next day with friends and co-workers. When the [[Argentina national football team]] plays (especially during world cup matches), streets tend to look completely deserted as everyone is watching the match.

But before that in the 1920s is when the culture around Argentina's men's football team started and it had something this to do with the mass media boom during that time. With the mass media boom and having the first generation of immigrant children born, the Argentina government decided to use the Argentina's men's football team as way to establish a connection with them and the country so they could be proud of their nationality. So the media wrote that the team played so well and has created its nation team style and with its attention grabbing headlines reached a very wide audience. With this style it continued and by October 1924 it ranked third in Buenos Aires many daily's. By then end of the decade it was selling 300,000 copies a day. And their way of reporting on football had a big effect on these statistics. According to "National Identity in the Sports Pages: Football and the Mass Media in 1920s Buenos Aires" by Matthew B. Karush.

It was in 1986 when the figure of [[Diego Maradona]] became well known internationally beyond the scope of just football. In Argentina, Maradona became a cultural icon. 

Supporters in Argentine football stadiums operate under a key principle known as ''Aguante'' (Endurance){{Clarify|reason=Wrong translation?|date=December 2022}} which serves as a belief system that guides the behavior of those in attendance. Key values that make up ''aguante'' that scholars such as ''Eduardo Herrera'' have also claimed are central in the construction of Argentine masculinity are courage, endurance, and fearlessness in physical confrontation.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018">Herrera, Eduardo. 2018. “Masculinity, Violence, and Deindividuation in Argentine Soccer Chants: The Sonic Potentials of Participatory Sounding-in-Synchrony.” Ethnomusicology 62(3): 470-499</ref> Fans can showcase these values when they are at stadiums in three significant way which are always supporting your team with your participation in chants and jumping throughout the match, attending literally every match that your team plays regardless of the circumstances, and standing your ground in the face of opposition insults or when engaged in any physical altercations at the stadium.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/>
It is under this principal of ''aguante'' that those in attendance of stadium matches in Argentina can be labeled under three broad categories which are ''hinchas'' (Fans), ''hinchinda militantes'' (militant fans), and ''espectadores'' (spectator).<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/> Those who classified as ''Hinchas'' exhibit many of the qualities under the ''aguante'' principle and often go to many of their team's matches, while ''hinchinda militantes'' who are usually found behind the goals with their team colors strictly follow what is asked of them under ''aguante'' by attending every one of their team's matches regardless of the weather or performance of the team.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/> The ''espectadores'' attend matches to enjoy the play of the game but do not weigh the principal of aguante close to heart compared the other two fan categories. Within the broad category of ''hinchinda militantes'' it is made up of la barra (supporters), ''la banda'' (the band), ''los pibes'' (the kids), and ''la pandilla'' (gang).<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/>
''La Barra'' is the central figure within the ''hinchinda militantes'' because of the critical role these subgroups of fans have in shaping the atmosphere of the stadium during matches and lead under a hierarchical structure with a capo (boss) at the top who organizes and tropes(followers) who heed the direction/instructions of the capo.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/> The leadership of these organized subgroups of fans, which are mainly made up of men between the ages of 15–50 years old, are entirely driven by demonstrations of aguante and awarded additional benefits stemming from relationships with club executives that grant special privileges to these groups such as tickets or allowing them to bring in typically prohibited items into the stadium to stir energy and excitement for the football club during the match. 
The excitement and passion at stadiums are typically found to be instigated and sustained by the presence of the percussion and brass instrument brought in by barras groups. The typical percussion instruments that are brought in and played by members of the barras at stadiums are the bombo con platillo (bass drum), Brazilian surdo drums, redoblantes (snare drums), repiques, scrappers, tambourines, cowbells, and agogo bells.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/> The brass instruments that are typically played at stadiums by outside musicians hired by barras groups are trumpets, trombones, and euphoniums.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/> While the collective energy and synchronization incited by the music can create a sense of unity among attendants and supporters alike, ethnomusicological scholar Eduardo Herrera also believes that they can embolden individuals to normalize discriminatory behavior that they wouldn't otherwise do if they weren't in a crowd, which would explain some of the recorded derogatory language and violent behavior found in Argentine stadiums.<ref name="Herrera, Eduardo 2018"/>

Argentine fans are not allowed to travel to see their teams in away matches, as they have been banned since 2013.<ref>{{cite news|title=Argentina bans football away supporters after fan death|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-22864505|access-date=24 March 2015|work=BBC News|date=12 June 2013|archive-date=11 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150311141147/http://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-22864505|url-status=live}}</ref>

''Hinchas'' (supporters) create an emotional ambiance in many stadiums, singing and cheering loudly all game long, but since the away fan ban due to violence, the atmosphere in many stadia has become less emotional, with goals for away teams greeted by silence and the disappearance of ''round trip chants'' between home and away fans, that provoked in each side to sing louder for show more passion.

''[[Barra brava]]s'' (Argentine organized groups – like the English [[hooligan firms]]) also create occasional problems, usually in riots after the match.
